item.title: Streamer Backlash Over Crash Photo: Kick’s Binx slammed for Miami plane stunt; legal fallout eyed
item.description: Kick streamer Binx is facing criticism after footage appeared to show her posing near the wreckage of an Amazon cargo plane that killed five people in Miami. The crash happened on September 6 after the Boeing 767-300 overran the runway and struck vehicles. Authorities are investigating the cause, while it remains unclear whether Binx could face any legal action over her access to the site.
item.dc:creator: Sumit Roy

item.title: Lindsay Clancy Mistrial: Hasan Piker rejects Polymarket ‘support’ claim; says stance miscast
item.description: Hasan Piker has denied Polymarket’s claim that he supports Lindsay Clancy, calling the wording a false description of his views. He has discussed Clancy’s postpartum psychosis defense, questioned her criminal responsibility and rejected theories blaming her husband. The case remains unresolved after a mistrial in Massachusetts, with prosecutors yet to decide whether Clancy will face another trial in the case.
item.dc:creator: Sumit Roy

item.title: Streamers Debate Emotions And Pain: IShowSpeed insists on nerve signals; Jasontheween says he feels pain daily
item.description: IShowSpeed and Jasontheween went viral after a surprising debate about emotions and pain during Jasontheween’s 72-hour collaboration video. Speed argued that emotions involve nerve signals and later suggested that pain is the brain processing physical signals at the atomic level. Jasontheween strongly disagreed with his unusual explanation. Their playful yet heated exchange quickly spread across social media, drawing attention from fans amused by their contrasting views.

item.title: In 1876, Jesse James’s gang tried to rob a Minnesota bank for seven minutes; 150 years later...
item.description: In a dramatic seven-minute standoff in Northfield, Minnesota, local citizens bravely confronted the notorious James-Younger Gang during a bank heist, ultimately leading to the gang's capture. Today, the Northfield Historical Society preserves fascinating artifacts, including an outlaw's duster and even a mummified ear from that fateful day. The town now honors this brave moment in history with a lively annual festival.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: At 16, an Indiana girl earned 5 cents a day working at a café; her family later bought it
item.description: South Bend's Sunny Italy Cafe, established in 1926, is celebrating its centennial anniversary. This historic eatery has remained under family ownership for a full century. The restaurant is renowned for its authentic, scratch-made Italian dishes and traditional recipes. Generations of Notre Dame students and local residents have frequented the establishment. Its enduring legacy highlights a unique culinary tradition in the community.

item.title: In 1952, Mary Tsingou programmed a Los Alamos experiment that helped change modern physics
item.description: In the 1950s, Mary Tsingou Menzel played a pivotal role in solving a complex physics problem using one of the earliest computers. Initially recognized only in a footnote for her computational work, her contributions to the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam problem have since gained fitting recognition. A true trailblazer in computational physics, she worked silently yet effectively in the realm of national security science.

item.title: Overdue Book Finally Returned: 1943 San Antonio loan arrives from Oregon; no late fee owed
item.description: After 82 years, a library book borrowed in 1943 was finally returned in Oregon, revealing a heartfelt letter detailing its extensive journey. The family inquired about overdue fees, but fortunately, the library had abolished such fines in 2021. The book, still in excellent condition, was briefly showcased before being put up for sale.

item.title: Scientists tagged 14,000 endangered moths with paint and glue; none turned up, and that may be good news
item.description: In a groundbreaking study, researchers have tagged over 14,000 Bogong moths in the Snowy Mountains of Australia. However, after extensive tracking efforts, none have been recaptured, suggesting potential populations larger than previously assumed. Alternatively, these moths might be utilizing undiscovered migration routes. The ongoing project remains crucial for understanding the ecology of these endangered insects.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Scientists covered 200 square metres of a Swiss glacier with sheep’s wool; early tests found...
item.description: In an innovative approach, Swiss researchers are experimenting with natural wool blankets to mitigate glacier melting. These eco-friendly coverings have shown results comparable to synthetic options during trials. The initiative makes use of discarded sheep's wool, an agricultural byproduct. Although effective in localized regions, it's important to note that this technique alone won't reverse global warming—tackling greenhouse gas emissions is essential for the long-term preservation of glaciers.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: An Australian woman learned she was pregnant and could give birth ‘any day’ within 24 hours
item.description: An Australian mother was shocked to find out she was pregnant just days before giving birth to a very premature baby. Her daughter, Makerita Tanuvasa, entered the world at just 21 weeks and three days, weighing only 351 grams. Remarkably, she became Australia’s most premature surviving infant. After more than four months in intensive care, receiving specialized treatment, she finally returned home, marking a miraculous recovery.
